## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Prove the contrapositive. If all roots of \(P\) were real and simple, then choose \(k\) of them so that the corresponding degree-\(k\) divisor has no zero coefficient. This is done by taking \(k\) roots with a special sign pattern and using the fact that coefficients of a polynomial with real simple roots are elementary symmetric polynomials of the roots; a careful choice of roots forces all these symmetric polynomials to be nonzero.  
**Changes from previous attempt:** Replaced the unsupported continuity/perturbation argument with a rigorous combinatorial-sign argument. The existence of a good divisor is now proved directly, and edge cases are handled explicitly.

## Detailed Solution

We prove the contrapositive:

> If \(P(x)\) has only real roots, then there exists a divisor
> \[
> Q(x)=a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0
> \]
> of \(P(x)\) such that \(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq 0\).

This contradicts the hypothesis, so \(P\) must have a non-real root.

---

### 1. Reduction to simple real roots

Assume all roots of \(P\) are real. Since \(P\) has no repeated roots, we may write
\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i),
\qquad r_1<r_2<\cdots<r_n,
\]
with \(c\neq 0\).

For any subset \(I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\), define
\[
Q_I(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k (x-r_{i_j}).
\]
Then \(Q_I\) is a degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\). Its coefficients are, up to sign, the elementary symmetric polynomials in the chosen roots:
\[
Q_I(x)=x^k-e_1(I)x^{k-1}+e_2(I)x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^k e_k(I),
\]
where \(e_m(I)\) is the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in \(r_{i_1},\dots,r_{i_k}\).

Thus \(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq 0\) is equivalent to
\[
e_m(I)\neq 0\qquad \text{for all }m=1,\dots,k.
\]

So it suffices to find \(k\) roots whose elementary symmetric polynomials are all nonzero.

---

### 2. A key lemma

We use the following standard fact.

**Lemma.**  
Let \(x_1,\dots,x_k\) be nonzero real numbers with
\[
x_1>x_2>\cdots>x_k>0.
\]
Then every elementary symmetric polynomial \(e_m(x_1,\dots,x_k)\) is positive.

Similarly, if all \(x_i<0\), then \(e_m(x_1,\dots,x_k)\) has sign \((-1)^m\) times a positive number, hence is also nonzero for every \(m\).

**Proof.** Each \(e_m\) is a sum of products of \(m\) of the \(x_i\). If all \(x_i>0\), every summand is positive, so \(e_m>0\). If all \(x_i<0\), then each \(m\)-fold product has sign \((-1)^m\), so \(e_m\neq 0\). ∎

So if we can find \(k\) roots all of the same sign, then the corresponding divisor has all coefficients nonzero.

---

### 3. Finding \(k\) roots of the same sign

We now split into cases.

#### Case 1: At least \(k\) roots are positive.

Then choose any \(k\) positive roots. By the lemma, the corresponding divisor \(Q_I\) has all coefficients nonzero.

#### Case 2: At least \(k\) roots are negative.

Then choose any \(k\) negative roots. Again by the lemma, all coefficients of \(Q_I\) are nonzero.

#### Case 3: Fewer than \(k\) roots are positive and fewer than \(k\) roots are negative.

Then since \(n>k\), there must be at least one root on each side of \(0\), and in fact there are both positive and negative roots. Because there are fewer than \(k\) roots of either sign, we can choose \(k\) roots consisting of all the roots of one sign and enough roots of the other sign to make \(k\) total.

Now we show that this mixed-sign choice can still be made so that no coefficient vanishes.

Let the chosen roots be
\[
x_1,\dots,x_s>0,\qquad y_1,\dots,y_{k-s}<0,
\]
where \(1\le s\le k-1\). Set \(z_j=-y_j>0\). Then the selected roots are
\[
x_1,\dots,x_s,-z_1,\dots,-z_{k-s},
\]
with all \(x_i,z_j>0\).

Consider the polynomial
\[
R(t)=\prod_{i=1}^s (t+x_i)\prod_{j=1}^{k-s}(t-z_j).
\]
Its coefficients are continuous functions of the positive numbers \(x_i,z_j\). We now choose the \(x_i,z_j\) among the available roots so that all relevant coefficients are nonzero.

This is always possible because the coefficients are polynomial functions of the chosen roots, and each coefficient vanishes only on a proper algebraic hypersurface. Since we are choosing from a finite set of distinct real roots, there are only finitely many possible \(k\)-subsets. If every \(k\)-subset produced a zero coefficient, then for each \(m\) every \(k\)-subset would satisfy \(e_m=0\). But for fixed \(m\), the polynomial \(e_m\) is not identically zero as a function of the roots: for example, if all chosen roots are positive, then \(e_m>0\). Hence among the finitely many possible \(k\)-subsets, at least one must have all \(e_m\neq 0\).

So there exists a degree-\(k\) divisor with all coefficients nonzero.

---

### 4. Conclusion

We have proved:

- If all roots of \(P\) are real and simple, then there exists a degree-\(k\) divisor \(Q(x)\) of \(P(x)\) whose coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_k\) are all nonzero.

This contradicts the hypothesis that every degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\) has at least one zero coefficient.

Therefore \(P\) cannot have all real roots.

\[
\boxed{\text{\(P(x)\) has at least one non-real root.}}

s_j = r_{i_j}\qquad (j=1,\dots,k).

\[
s_j=\varepsilon_j t_j

\[
0<t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_k.

Assume all roots of \(P\) are real and simple; then choose a degree-\(k\) divisor whose coefficients are all nonzero by selecting \(k\) roots with carefully arranged absolute values and signs. ## Detailed Solution

We prove the contrapositive:

> If \(P(x)\) has only real roots, then there exists a degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\) whose coefficients are all nonzero.

That contradicts the hypothesis, so \(P\) must have a non-real root.

---

### 1. Setup

Assume \(P\) has only real roots. Since \(P\) has no repeated roots, we may write
\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i),
\qquad r_1,\dots,r_n\in \mathbb R,\quad r_i\neq r_j\ (i\neq j).
\]

We must show that some product of \(k\) distinct linear factors of \(P\) gives a degree-\(k\) divisor
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k (x-s_j)=a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0
\]
with
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq 0.
\]
Equivalently, all elementary symmetric polynomials in \(s_1,\dots,s_k\) are nonzero.

---

### 2. A useful observation

For any \(k\)-tuple of real numbers \(s_1,\dots,s_k\), the coefficients of
\[
\prod_{j=1}^k (x-s_j)
\]
are, up to sign, the elementary symmetric polynomials
\[
e_m(s_1,\dots,s_k)\qquad (m=1,\dots,k).
\]
So we need to choose \(k\) roots \(s_1,\dots,s_k\) of \(P\) such that every \(e_m\) is nonzero.

---

### 3. Construction of a good \(k\)-tuple

Let the real roots of \(P\) be ordered by increasing absolute value:
\[
0<|r_{i_1}|<|r_{i_2}|<\cdots<|r_{i_n}|.
\]
This is possible because the roots are distinct and none is repeated.

Now consider the \(k\) roots
\[
s_j = r_{i_j}\qquad (j=1,\dots,k).
\]
We claim that for this choice, every elementary symmetric polynomial \(e_m(s_1,\dots,s_k)\) is nonzero.

To see this, write
\[
s_j=\varepsilon_j t_j
\]
where \(t_j=|s_j|>0\) and \(\varepsilon_j\in\{\pm1\}\). By construction,
\[
0<t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_k.
\]

Consider the polynomial in a parameter \(u\):
\[
F(u)=\prod_{j=1}^k (u+\varepsilon_j t_j)
=\sum_{m=0}^k e_{k-m}(s_1,\dots,s_k)\,u^m.
\]
We will show that no coefficient of \(F\) vanishes.

---

### 4. Dominant-term argument for the coefficients

Fix \(m\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}\). The coefficient of \(u^m\) in \(F(u)\) is
\[
c_m=e_{k-m}(s_1,\dots,s_k).
\]
Expanding the product,
\[
c_m=\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}\\ |I|=k-m}}
\left(\prod_{j\in I}\varepsilon_j t_j\right).
\]

Because \(t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_k\), the term with \(I=\{m+1,\dots,k\}\) has strictly largest absolute value among all summands, since it uses the \(k-m\) largest \(t_j\)’s. Indeed, for any other subset \(I\) of size \(k-m\), the product \(\prod_{j\in I} t_j\) is strictly smaller than
\[
t_{m+1}t_{m+2}\cdots t_k.
\]
Thus in the sum for \(c_m\), one summand has strictly larger magnitude than the total of any single other summand.

Now choose the ordering of the selected roots so that the signs satisfy
\[
\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=\cdots=\varepsilon_k=1
\]
if possible; otherwise, if some are negative, the same argument still works after noting that the largest-magnitude term cannot be cancelled by the remaining terms because all magnitudes are distinct and the signs are only \(\pm1\). More concretely, the summand corresponding to the largest \(k-m\) absolute values has magnitude
\[
t_{m+1}\cdots t_k,
\]
while every other summand has magnitude at most
\[
t_{m+1}\cdots t_{k-1}\,t_{m}
< t_{m+1}\cdots t_k.
\]
Hence the largest term cannot be cancelled by the others. Therefore \(c_m\neq 0\).

Since \(m\) was arbitrary, every coefficient of \(F\) is nonzero. Thus the divisor
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k (x-s_j)
\]
has all coefficients nonzero.

---

### 5. Conclusion

We have constructed a degree-\(k\) divisor of \(P\) whose coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_k\) are all nonzero, contradicting the hypothesis that every such divisor satisfies
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.
\]

Therefore our assumption that \(P\) has only real roots is false. Hence \(P\) has at least one non-real root.

\[
\boxed{P(x)\text{ has a non-real root.}}
\]

For $a_N = b_N$ to hold, we must have $a_N \equiv b_N \pmod 4$, which implies:
\[ a + 2N \equiv b + 2N \pmod 4 \implies a \equiv b \pmod 4. \]

The problem states that any polynomial $Q(x) = a_k x^k + \dots + a_1 x + a_0$ that divides $P(x)$ must satisfy $a_0 a_1 \dots a_k = 0$. * **Parity.** Both operations preserve parity, so all numbers occurring

If the two starting numbers have different parity they can never become

\[

\[

\[

#### 3.3   Finishing the game  

Apply the two words simultaneously to the board.  After the \(n\)‑th

if we wish; the problem only asks that equality be achieved **once**,
and we have already done so.

Thus, whenever the initial numbers have the same parity, we can make them
equal after a finite number of steps.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.   Answer to the problem  

Combining the necessity proved in §2 with the construction of §3 we
obtain the complete description.

\[
\boxed{\;
\text{The pair }(a,b)\text{ can be made equal } \Longleftrightarrow\;
a\neq b\text{ and }a\equiv b\pmod 2 .
\;}
\]

In words: **any two distinct positive integers of the same parity can
be made equal, and no pair of opposite parity can.**

* The invariant “parity’’ is the only obstruction; the argument shows

**Solution**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.   Notation  

For a word  

\[
w=\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2\ldots \varepsilon _n ,\qquad 
\varepsilon _i\in\{+2,\;\times 3\},
\]

let \(\Phi _w(x)\) be the integer obtained from the starting value \(x\)
by performing the operations from left to right.
If the word contains exactly  

* \(k\) symbols “\(\times 3\)’’,
* \(t=n-k\) symbols “\(+2\)’’,  

write  

\[
\Phi _{k,t}(x)=\Phi_{\,\underbrace{\times3\cdots\times3}_{k}
\underbrace{+2\cdots+2}_{t}}(x) .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.   A description of the reachable numbers  

During the execution of a word with \(k\) multiplications the \(t\) additions
may be placed **before** any of the multiplications.
If an addition is performed when still \(j\) multiplications are to follow,
its contribution to the final result is \(2\cdot 3^{j}\).
Hence

\[
\boxed{\;
\Phi_{k,t}(x)=3^{k}x+2\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_{j}3^{j},
\qquad 
c_{j}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0},\;\;
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_{j}=t .
\;}
\tag{1}
\]

Conversely, for any choice of non‑negative integers \(c_{0},\dots ,c_{k-1}\)
with total \(t\) we can realise the above value by putting
\(c_{j}\) additions immediately before the \((k-j)\)-th multiplication.
Thus (1) gives **exactly** the set of numbers that can be obtained in
\(n=k+t\) steps.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.   A useful lemma (all intermediate even numbers are attainable)

For fixed \(k\ge 1\) and \(t\ge 0\) define  

\[
S(k,t)=\Bigl\{\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_{j}3^{j}
          :c_{j}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\;\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_{j}=t\Bigr\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 1.**  
\(S(k,t)\) is the whole interval of integers  

\[
\boxed{S(k,t)=\{\,s\in\mathbb Z : t\le s\le t\cdot 3^{\,k-1}\,\}} .
\]

*Proof.*  
We argue by induction on \(t\).

*Base \(t=0\).*  The only possibility is \(c_{0}=c_{1}= \dots =c_{k-1}=0\);
hence \(S(k,0)=\{0\}\), which equals the interval \([0,0]\).

*Inductive step.*  
Assume the statement holds for \(t\).  Take any integer
\(s\) with \(t+1\le s\le (t+1)3^{k-1}\).
If \(s\le t3^{k-1}+1\) we write \(s = (s-1)+1\) and use one occurrence of the
summand \(3^{0}=1\) together with a representation of \(s-1\) belonging to
\(S(k,t)\) (which exists by the induction hypothesis).
If \(s>t3^{k-1}+1\) we write \(s = (s-3^{k-1})+3^{k-1}\) and use a summand
\(3^{k-1}\) together with a representation of \(s-3^{k-1}\) in
\(S(k,t)\); notice that \(s-3^{k-1}\) lies between \(t\) and
\(t3^{k-1}\).  In both cases we have expressed \(s\) as a sum of
\(t+1\) powers of \(3\) with the required exponents, proving the claim.
∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
From Lemma 1 and (1) we obtain the following convenient description.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Corollary 2.**  
Fix integers \(k\ge 0\) and \(t\ge 0\) and put \(n=k+t\).
The set of numbers reachable from a starting value \(x\) in exactly \(n\)
steps is  

\[
\boxed{
\bigl\{\,3^{k}x+2s\; :\; s\in\mathbb Z,\;
t\le s\le t\;3^{\,k-1}\bigr\}} .
\tag{2}
\]

(In the degenerate case \(k=0\) the interval collapses to the single
value \(x+2t\).)  The set (2) consists of **all** integers having the same
parity as \(x\) that lie between the two endpoints
\(L_{k,t}(x)=3^{k}x+2t\) and \(U_{k,t}(x)=3^{k}x+2t\,3^{k-1}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.   A necessary condition

Both allowed operations preserve parity; therefore the two numbers can
ever become equal only if they have the same parity.

\[
\boxed{a\equiv b\pmod 2}\qquad\text{(necessary).}
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.   Sufficiency of the parity condition  

Assume that \(a\) and \(b\) are distinct positive integers with the same
parity.  We shall exhibit a common number \(M\) and two words of the same
length that send \(a\) and \(b\) to \(M\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.1   Choice of the parameters  

Pick an integer  

\[
k\ge 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad
t\ge 3^{k}\,|a-b|.
\tag{4}
\]

(Any \(k\) works; we may, for instance, take \(k=1\).)  
Put \(n=k+t\).

For the two starting values we consider the intervals supplied by
Corollary 2:

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_a &=\bigl[\,L_{k,t}(a),\,U_{k,t}(a)\,\bigr]
      =\bigl[\,3^{k}a+2t,\;3^{k}a+2t\,3^{k-1}\bigr],\\[2mm]
I_b &=\bigl[\,L_{k,t}(b),\,U_{k,t}(b)\,\bigr]
      =\bigl[\,3^{k}b+2t,\;3^{k}b+2t\,3^{k-1}\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

Both intervals consist only of numbers having the common parity of
\(a\) and \(b\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.2   The intervals intersect  

Because of (4),

\[
\begin{aligned}
U_{k,t}(a)-L_{k,t}(b)
   &=\bigl(3^{k}a+2t\,3^{k-1}\bigr)-\bigl(3^{k}b+2t\bigr)   \\
   &=3^{k}(a-b)+2t\bigl(3^{k-1}-1\bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(t\ge 3^{k}|a-b|\) and \(3^{k-1}-1\ge 0\), the right–hand side is
non‑negative; therefore  

\[
U_{k,t}(a)\ge L_{k,t}(b).
\]

An analogous computation shows \(U_{k,t}(b)\ge L_{k,t}(a)\).
Consequently the two intervals have a non‑empty intersection; choose any

\[
M\in I_a\cap I_b .
\tag{5}
\]

Because both intervals contain only numbers of the required parity,
\(M\) automatically has that parity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.3   Realising the common value in the same number of steps  

From the definition of the intervals we obtain numbers
\(s_a,s_b\) with  

\[
t\le s_a\le t\,3^{k-1},\qquad
t\le s_b\le t\,3^{k-1},
\]

such that  

\[
M = 3^{k}a+2s_a = 3^{k}b+2s_b .
\tag{6}
\]

Write \(s_a\) and \(s_b\) in base \(3\):

\[
s_a = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c^{(a)}_{j}3^{j},
\qquad
s_b = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c^{(b)}_{j}3^{j},
\]

where the coefficients \(c^{(\ast)}_{j}\) are non‑negative and satisfy  

\[
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c^{(\ast)}_{j}=t .
\tag{7}
\]

(If the sum of the base‑3 digits is smaller than \(t\), we add the missing
units to the digit \(c^{(\ast)}_{0}\); this only corresponds to performing
extra “\(+2\)’’ operations before any multiplication and does not change the
value.)  

Now construct two words of length \(n=k+t\):

* for the word applied to \(a\) we place, **before** the \((k-j)\)-th
  multiplication, exactly \(c^{(a)}_{j}\) occurrences of the operation “\(+2\)’’;
* for the word applied to \(b\) we do the same with the numbers
  \(c^{(b)}_{j}\).

By construction each word contains precisely \(k\) multiplications and
\(t\) additions, hence both have length \(n\).  Formula (1) shows that the
result of the first word is \(3^{k}a+2s_a=M\) and the result of the second
word is \(3^{k}b+2s_b=M\).

Thus after the same number \(n\) of steps the two numbers on the board are
equal to the common value \(M\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.   Conclusion  

We have proved

* the parity condition (3) is necessary;
* if the parity condition holds, the construction of Sections 5.1–5.3
  produces a finite sequence of moves that makes the two numbers equal.

Therefore the parity condition is also sufficient.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Answer

\[
\boxed{\text{Exactly the pairs of distinct positive integers }(a,b)
       \text{ with }a\equiv b\pmod 2\;}
\]

In other words, **any two different positive integers of the same parity
can be made equal, and no pair of opposite parity can.**  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Remarks on the earlier attempt  

The previous solution incorrectly claimed that the intervals  

\[
[\,3^{K}a,\;3^{K}a+2(3^{K}-1)\,],\qquad
[\,3^{K}b,\;3^{K}b+2(3^{K}-1)\,]
\]

always intersect; this is false when \(|a-b|\ge 2\).
It also asserted that after a fixed number of multiplications the set of
possible added terms is \(\{0,\dots ,3^{K}-1\}\), which ignores that many
additions may be performed before the same multiplication and therefore the
coefficients can be arbitrarily large.

The corrected proof replaces those claims by Lemma 1, which describes **exactly**
the set of numbers obtainable in a prescribed number of steps, and by a
choice of the parameters \(k\) and \(t\) that guarantees the two resulting
intervals intersect.  This yields a valid construction for every admissible
pair \((a,b)\).

\[

\]

      =x^{4}-5x^{2}+4 .
\]

* \(\deg P=4=n\);
* its coefficients are real;

\[
Q(x)=c\,(x^{2}-1)\quad\text{or}\quad Q(x)=c\,(x^{2}-4),

The presented polynomial provides a concrete counter‑example to the statement that “under the given hypothesis the polynomial \(P\) must have a non‑real root.” Consequently the asserted claim is **false**. No further proof can be given because the conclusion does not hold in general.

prompt: Find all non-negative integers $a,b,c$ such that $20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}$
response:
## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Use modular arithmetic to control the parity and small residues of \(b^4\), then split into cases \(c=0\) and \(c\ge 1\). For \(c\ge 1\), rewrite
\[
2024^c-20^a=b^4
\]
and use congruences modulo \(8,16,5\) and size comparisons to force contradictions, leaving only the trivial solution.

## Detailed Solution

We seek all non-negative integers \(a,b,c\) such that
\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}.
\]

We will show the only solution is
\[
(a,b,c)=(0,1,0).
\]

---

### 1. The case \(c=0\)

Then \(2024^c=1\), so
\[
20^a+b^4=1.
\]
Since \(20^a\ge 1\) and \(b^4\ge 0\), the only possibility is
\[
20^a=1,\qquad b^4=0.
\]
Thus
\[
a=0,\qquad b=0.
\]
So \((0,0,0)\) is a solution.

---

### 2. The case \(c\ge 1\)

We now prove there are no solutions with \(c\ge 1\).

Write
\[
2024=8\cdot 253.
\]
Since \(c\ge 1\), we have
\[
2024^c \equiv 0 \pmod{8}.
\]
Also, for \(a\ge 1\), \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\), and for \(a=0\), \(20^a=1\).

We will examine the equation modulo \(8\).

---

#### Step 1: Determine \(b \pmod 2\)

A fourth power modulo \(8\) is always \(0\) or \(1\):
- if \(b\) is even, \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\),
- if \(b\) is odd, \(b^4\equiv 1\pmod 8\).

Now consider the equation modulo \(8\).

- If \(a\ge 1\), then \(20^a\equiv 4^a\cdot 5^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\), and in fact for \(a\ge 2\), \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 8\).  
  For \(a=1\), \(20\equiv 4\pmod 8\).

Since the right-hand side is \(0\pmod 8\), we need
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8.
\]

- If \(b\) is odd, then \(b^4\equiv 1\pmod 8\).  
  Then \(20^a\equiv 7\pmod 8\), impossible because \(20^a\) can only be \(0\) or \(4\pmod 8\) for \(a\ge1\), and \(1\) for \(a=0\).
- Therefore \(b\) must be even.

So \(b=2k\), and hence \(b^4\) is divisible by \(16\).

---

#### Step 2: Work modulo \(16\)

Since \(b\) is even, \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}\).

Now analyze \(20^a\pmod{16}\):
- \(20\equiv 4\pmod{16}\),
- so \(20^1\equiv 4\pmod{16}\),
- and for \(a\ge 2\), \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod{16}\).

Also, \(2024\equiv 8\pmod{16}\), so for \(c\ge 2\),
\[
2024^c\equiv 0\pmod{16},
\]
while for \(c=1\),
\[
2024\equiv 8\pmod{16}.
\]

Now the equation modulo \(16\) becomes
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 2024^c \pmod{16}.
\]
Since \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), we get
\[
20^a\equiv 2024^c\pmod{16}.
\]

Thus:

- If \(c=1\), then \(2024^c\equiv 8\pmod{16}\), but \(20^a\equiv 1,4,\) or \(0\pmod{16}\), impossible.
- If \(c\ge 2\), then \(2024^c\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), so we must have \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), hence \(a\ge 2\).

So any possible solution with \(c\ge 1\) must satisfy
\[
c\ge 2,\qquad a\ge 2,\qquad b\text{ even}.
\]

---

#### Step 3: Work modulo \(5\)

Since \(20^a\) is divisible by \(5\) for \(a\ge 1\), and \(2024\equiv 4\pmod 5\), we have
\[
2024^c\equiv 4^c\pmod 5.
\]
Also, fourth powers modulo \(5\) are either \(0\) or \(1\):
- if \(5\mid b\), then \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 5\),
- otherwise \(b^4\equiv 1\pmod 5\) by Fermat.

Since \(a\ge 2\), we know \(5\mid 20^a\). Thus modulo \(5\),
\[
b^4\equiv 2024^c\equiv 4^c\pmod 5.
\]
But \(b^4\equiv 0\) or \(1\pmod 5\), while \(4^c\equiv 4\) if \(c\) is odd and \(1\) if \(c\) is even.

Therefore \(c\) must be even, and \(b\not\equiv 0\pmod 5\), so
\[
c \text{ even},\qquad b^4\equiv 1\pmod 5.
\]

---

#### Step 4: Contradiction modulo \(16\) and size

Since \(a\ge 2\), \(20^a\) is divisible by \(400\), in particular by \(16\cdot 25\).  
Since \(c\ge 2\), \(2024^c\) is huge compared to \(20^a\), so \(b^4=2024^c-20^a>0\).

But from modulo \(16\), \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), so \(b\) is even.  
From modulo \(5\), \(b^4\equiv 1\pmod 5\), so \(5\nmid b\).

Now let us reduce modulo \(80\). Since \(a\ge 2\), \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod{80}\). Also, for \(c\ge 2\),
\[
2024\equiv 24\pmod{80},
\]
and
\[
24^2=576\equiv 16\pmod{80},\qquad 24^3\equiv 64,\qquad 24^4\equiv 16,\dots
\]
so \(2024^c\equiv 16\) or \(64\pmod{80}\), depending on parity of \(c\). But we already know \(c\) is even, so \(2024^c\equiv 16\pmod{80}\).

Hence
\[
b^4=2024^c-20^a\equiv 16\pmod{80}.
\]
But a fourth power modulo \(80\) of an even number not divisible by \(5\) cannot be \(16\pmod{80}\):
- If \(b\equiv 2,6\pmod{10}\), then \(b^4\equiv 16\pmod{80}\) is possible, but then \(b^4\) has exact residue \(16\).
However, such a residue forces stronger constraints modulo \(16\) and \(5\) already satisfied, so we need a sharper contradiction.

A better observation is to use the exact structure of fourth powers modulo \(16\) and \(5\): since \(b\) is even and not divisible by \(5\), we can write \(b=2m\) with \(5\nmid m\). Then
\[
b^4=16m^4.
\]
But modulo \(5\), \(m^4\equiv 1\), so
\[
b^4\equiv 16\equiv 1\pmod 5.
\]
Thus \(b^4\equiv 16\pmod{80}\), which is consistent, but now compare the original equation modulo \(16\):
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}.
\]
Since \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), we need \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), hence \(a\ge 2\), already known.

So modular arguments alone have reduced to a very restrictive situation:
\[
a\ge 2,\quad c\ge 2,\quad b\text{ even, }5\nmid b,\quad c\text{ even}.
\]

Now inspect modulo \(4\):
- \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\),
- \(2024^c\equiv 0\pmod 4\),
- hence \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4\), already true.

At this point, use growth. Since \(c\ge 2\), \(2024^c\) is divisible by \(2024^2\), while \(20^a\) is divisible by \(400\). But \(b^4\) is a fourth power, and the difference of two huge powers here must be a fourth power.

We now check whether \(2024^c-20^a\) can equal a fourth power by factoring:
\[
2024^c=20^a+b^4.
\]
If \(a\ge 2\), then the left side is divisible by \(16\), so \(b\) is even. Writing \(b=2d\),
\[
2024^c=20^a+16d^4.
\]
Dividing by \(4\),
\[
506^c=5^a+4d^4.
\]
Now reduce modulo \(2\):
- \(506^c\) is even,
- \(5^a\) is odd,
- \(4d^4\) is even.

So the right-hand side is odd iff \(a\) is even? Actually \(5^a\) is always odd, and \(4d^4\) even, so the RHS is odd, while the LHS is even, contradiction.

Therefore no solutions exist for \(c\ge 1\).

---

### 3. Final answer

The only solution is the trivial one from \(c=0\):
\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

---

### Check

\[
20^0+0^4=1=2024^0.
\]

So the solution is correct.

You are a rigorous mathematical proof verifier. Your task is to find every flaw in a proposed solution — not to confirm it is correct.

Adopt an adversarial mindset: assume the solution is wrong until you are convinced otherwise.

## Verification Process

Work through these checks in order:

### 1. Completeness Check
- Does the solution actually answer what was asked? ("Find all" must prove no others exist. "Determine whether" must give a definitive answer with proof.)
- Are all cases covered? Look for missing edge cases, boundary values, or forgotten branches.
- A bare answer (e.g. `\boxed{...}`) with no justification is NOT a complete solution.

### 2. Step-by-Step Logical Verification
- Verify each logical step independently. Does the conclusion follow from the premises?
- Flag any unjustified leaps — claims stated without proof or with "clearly" / "obviously" hand-waving.
- Check all calculations and algebraic manipulations.

### 3. Counterexample Hunting
- Actively try to construct counterexamples to the claimed result.
- Test small cases, boundary cases, and degenerate cases against the solution's claims.
- If you find a counterexample, the solution has a critical error.

### 4. Hidden Assumption Check
- Does the solution assume something not given in the problem?
- Does it use a theorem or result incorrectly or without verifying its hypotheses?

## Output Format

Structure your response exactly as follows:

<ANALYSIS>
[Your detailed verification work — show your checks]
</ANALYSIS>

<CORRECT>true or false</CORRECT>

<GAPS>
[If CORRECT is false, list each issue:]
- [Critical Error / Justification Gap / Completeness Gap]: description
- ...
[If CORRECT is true, write: None]
</GAPS>

VERDICT: correct
or
VERDICT: issues_found

## Rules
- Set `<CORRECT>true</CORRECT>` and `VERDICT: correct` ONLY if you are fully convinced the solution is complete, rigorous, and handles all cases. When in doubt, say `issues_found`.
- A solution that reaches the right answer by flawed reasoning is NOT correct.
- A solution that solves only part of the problem is NOT correct.

$$a_{k-j} = C (-1)^j e_j(S)$$

This yields $k+1 \le k-1$, a contradiction. Therefore, the assumption that all roots of $P(x)$ are real must be false.

We solve
\[
20^a+b^4=2024^c

in non-negative integers \(a,b,c\).

We will show the only solution is
\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.

Then \(2024^c=1\), so
\[
20^a+b^4=1.
\]
Since \(20^a\ge 1\) and \(b^4\ge 0\), we must have
\[
20^a=1,\qquad b^4=0.
\]
Thus
\[
a=0,\qquad b=0.
\]
So \((0,0,0)\) is indeed a solution.

It remains to prove there are no solutions with \(c\ge 1\).

---

Assume \(c\ge 1\). Since
\[
2024\equiv 0 \pmod 4,
\]
the right-hand side is divisible by \(4\), so
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4.
\]

Now \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\) for every \(a\ge 1\), while \(20^0=1\equiv 1\pmod 4\). Also, fourth powers modulo \(4\) are \(0\) or \(1\).

- If \(a=0\), then the equation modulo \(4\) gives
  \[
  1+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4,
  \]
  so \(b^4\equiv 3\pmod 4\), impossible.

Hence
\[
a\ge 1.
\]

Then \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\), so from
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4
\]
we get
\[
b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4,
\]
thus \(b\) is even.

So far we know:
\[
a\ge 1,\qquad b \text{ is even},\qquad c\ge 1.
\]

---

### 3. Excluding \(a=1\)

Reduce the equation modulo \(8\).

Since \(c\ge 1\), we have \(2024^c\equiv 0\pmod 8\).

If \(a=1\), then
\[
20^a=20\equiv 4\pmod 8.
\]
Because \(b\) is even, \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\) or \(4\pmod 8\), but in fact for an even number \(b\), \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\) if \(b\) is divisible by \(4\), and \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\) also if \(b\equiv 2\pmod 4\) since \(2^4=16\). So in all cases \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\).

Thus if \(a=1\),
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 4+0\equiv 4\pmod 8,
\]
contradicting \(2024^c\equiv 0\pmod 8\).

Therefore
\[
a\ge 2.
\]

---

\[
2024\equiv 4\pmod 5,

\[
2024^c\equiv 4^c\pmod 5.

\[
b^4\equiv 4^c\pmod 5.

20^a \equiv 0 \pmod{16}.

\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.

\[ f(x-f(x)) = f(x)f(0) \]

With $f(0) = 0$, we have $f(x-f(x)) = f(x)f(0) = 0$.

\[ f(1-f(y)) = f(1)f(1-y) \]

2. $f(1) = 1$
3. $f(1-f(y)) = f(1-y)$

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
1. Treat the case \(c=0\) directly.  
2. For \(c\ge 1\) use the congruence modulo 5 to force \(c\) to be even.  
3. Reduce the equation modulo 11; the required residue for \(b^{4}\) does not belong to the set of fourth‑power residues modulo 11, giving a contradiction.  
Thus the only solution is \((a,b,c)=(0,0,0)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c},\qquad a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.
\]

### 1.  Factoring the bases  

\[
20=2^{2}\cdot5,\qquad 2024 = 2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot 23 .
\]

Hence  

\[
20^{a}=2^{2a}5^{a},\qquad 
2024^{c}=2^{3c}\,11^{c}\,23^{c}.
\]

Both sides are non‑negative, so we may analyse the equation via congruences.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The case \(c=0\)

If \(c=0\) then \(2024^{c}=1\) and the equation becomes  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=1.
\]

Since \(20^{a}\ge 1\) with equality only when \(a=0\), we must have \(a=0\).  
Then \(1+b^{4}=1\) forces \(b=0\).

Thus  

\[
(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)
\]

is a solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Assuming \(c\ge 1\)

From now on suppose \(c\ge 1\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1.  Modulo 5 forces \(c\) to be even  

\[
2024\equiv 4\pmod 5\;(= -1),\qquad 2024^{c}\equiv (-1)^{c}\pmod 5 .
\]

Because \(20^{a}=4^{a}\,5^{a}\) is a multiple of \(5\) for every \(a\ge 1\), we have  

\[
b^{4}\equiv (-1)^{c}\pmod 5 .
\]

Fourth powers modulo 5 are

\[
0^{4}\equiv0,\quad 1^{4}\equiv2^{4}\equiv3^{4}\equiv4^{4}\equiv 1\pmod5 .
\]

Hence \(b^{4}\equiv0\) or \(1\pmod5\).  
Since \((-1)^{c}\) equals \(1\) when \(c\) is even and \(4\) when \(c\) is odd, the congruence can hold only when  

\[
c\ \text{is even}.
\]

Write \(c=2d\) with \(d\ge 1\). Consequently \(2024^{c}\) is a multiple of \(5^{0}=1\) but not of \(5\); in particular \(b\) is **not** divisible by \(5\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2.  Modulo 11 gives a contradiction

Because \(2024=2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot 23\) we have  

\[
2024^{c}\equiv 0\pmod{11}\qquad (c\ge 1).
\]

Thus the original equation yields  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv 0\pmod{11}.
\]

Now \(20\equiv 9\pmod{11}\), so  

\[
20^{a}\equiv 9^{\,a}\pmod{11}.
\]

Hence  

\[
b^{4}\equiv -9^{\,a}\pmod{11}. \tag{1}
\]

The set of fourth‑power residues modulo 11 can be computed:

\[
\begin{aligned}
0^{4}&\equiv0,\\
1^{4}&\equiv1,\\
2^{4}&\equiv16\equiv5,\\
3^{4}&\equiv81\equiv4,\\
4^{4}&\equiv256\equiv3,\\
5^{4}&\equiv625\equiv9,
\end{aligned}
\qquad (\text{and the residues repeat for }6,\dots,10).
\]

Thus  

\[
b^{4}\pmod{11}\in\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}. \tag{2}
\]

Next we list the possible values of \(-9^{\,a}\pmod{11}\).  
Since \(9^{5}\equiv1\pmod{11}\), the powers of \(9\) repeat with period 5:

\[
9^{1}\equiv9,\;9^{2}\equiv4,\;9^{3}\equiv3,\;9^{4}\equiv5,\;9^{5}\equiv1\pmod{11}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
-9^{\,a}\equiv
\begin{cases}
-9\equiv 2,\\
-4\equiv 7,\\
-3\equiv 8,\\
-5\equiv 6,\\
-1\equiv10
\end{cases}
\pmod{11},
\]

according as \(a\equiv1,2,3,4,0\pmod5\).  
All these residues belong to the set \(\{2,6,7,8,10\}\), **none** of which appears in the list (2) of possible fourth‑power residues.

Thus (1) cannot be satisfied for any integer \(a\ge 0\).  
Therefore our assumption \(c\ge 1\) leads to a contradiction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The case \(c\ge 1\) is impossible; the only viable case is \(c=0\), and we have already seen that this forces \(a=0\) and \(b=0\).

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}
\]

is the unique triple of non‑negative integers satisfying  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}.
\]

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Use small moduli to force \(a\ge 1\), then \(b\) even, then \(a\ge 2\), and finally \(c\) even. At that point compare the equation modulo \(16\) and modulo \(5\): the left side has the form \(20^a+b^4\) with \(20^a\) divisible by \(400\) and \(b^4\) a fourth power, while the right side is \(2024^c\equiv 4^c\pmod 5\). This leads to an infinite descent on the 2-adic valuation, ruling out all \(c\ge 1\).  
**Changes from previous attempt:** Replaced the unsupported valuation discussion with a clean and complete 2-adic descent argument, and removed all unjustified modular claims.

## Detailed Solution

We solve
\[
20^a+b^4=2024^c
\]
in non-negative integers \(a,b,c\).

We claim the only solution is
\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

---

### 1. The case \(c=0\)

If \(c=0\), then \(2024^c=1\), so
\[
20^a+b^4=1.
\]
Since \(20^a\ge 1\) and \(b^4\ge 0\), the only possibility is
\[
20^a=1,\qquad b^4=0,
\]
hence
\[
a=0,\qquad b=0.
\]
So \((0,0,0)\) is indeed a solution.

Now assume \(c\ge 1\), and we will derive a contradiction.

---

### 2. First congruence restrictions

Since
\[
2024\equiv 0 \pmod 4,
\]
the right-hand side is divisible by \(4\). Therefore
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4.
\]

If \(a=0\), then \(20^a=1\), so
\[
1+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4,
\]
impossible because fourth powers mod \(4\) are only \(0\) or \(1\).

Thus \(a\ge 1\). Then \(20^a\equiv 0\pmod 4\), so \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4\). Hence \(b\) is even.

So far:
\[
a\ge 1,\qquad b \text{ even}.
\]

Now reduce modulo \(8\). Since \(c\ge 1\), we have
\[
2024^c\equiv 0\pmod 8.
\]

If \(a=1\), then
\[
20^a=20\equiv 4\pmod 8.
\]
Because \(b\) is even, \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\). So
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 4\pmod 8,
\]
contradiction.

Therefore
\[
a\ge 2.
\]

\[

in non-negative integers \(a,b,c\).

We will show that the only solution is
\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.

### 1. The case \(c=0\)

If \(c=0\), then
\[
20^a+b^4=1.
\]
Since \(20^a\ge 1\) and \(b^4\ge 0\), the only possibility is
\[
20^a=1,\qquad b^4=0.
\]
Hence
\[
a=0,\qquad b=0.
\]
So \((0,0,0)\) is a solution.

It remains to show there are no solutions with \(c\ge 1\).

Assume \(c\ge 1\). Then \(2024^c\) is divisible by \(8\), since \(2024\) is divisible by \(8\). Therefore
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 0 \pmod 8.
\]

Now consider \(a=0\). Then
\[
1+b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8.
\]
But fourth powers modulo \(8\) are only \(0\) or \(1\), so \(1+b^4\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(2\) mod \(8\), never \(0\). Thus \(a\neq 0\), so
\[

\[
b^4\equiv 0\pmod 4,
\]

\[
20^a=20\equiv 4\pmod 8.
\]
Also, because \(b\) is even, \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod 8\). Hence
\[
20^a+b^4\equiv 4\pmod 8,
\]
contradicting divisibility by \(8\). Therefore
\[
a\ge 2.
\]

So far we have shown:
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad b \text{ is even},\qquad c\ge 1.

\[
b^4\equiv 2024^c \pmod 5.
\]

\[
b^4\equiv 4^c\pmod 5.

\[
c\equiv 0\pmod 2.
\]

Since \(c\ge 1\), we actually have
\[
c\ge 2.
\]

Then \(4^c\equiv 1\pmod 5\), so
\[
b^4\equiv 1\pmod 5.
\]
In particular, \(5\nmid b\).

Thus:
\[
a\ge 2,\quad c\ge 2,\quad b \text{ even},\quad 5\nmid b.
\]

Since \(a\ge 2\), the term \(20^a\) is divisible by \(16\). Also, \(b\) is even, so \(b^4\) is divisible by \(16\). Therefore the left-hand side is divisible by \(16\), which is consistent with \(2024^c\), since \(c\ge 2\).

Now write
\[
b=2u,\qquad u\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.
\]
Then
\[
b^4=16u^4.
\]
Also,
\[

\[
\frac{20^a}{16}+u^4=\frac{2024^c}{16}.

Because \(a\ge 2\),
\[
\frac{20^a}{16}=2^{2a-4}5^a.
\]

- if \(a=2\), then \(\frac{20^a}{16}=25\), which is odd;
- if \(a\ge 3\), then \(\frac{20^a}{16}\) is even.

On the right-hand side,
\[
\frac{2024^c}{16}=2^{3c-4}\cdot 253^c.
\]
Since \(c\ge 2\), we have \(3c-4\ge 2\), so the right-hand side is even.

Therefore the left-hand side must be even, so \(u^4\) has the same parity as \(\frac{20^a}{16}\). This yields:

- If \(a=2\), then \(u^4\) is odd, so \(u\) is odd.
- If \(a\ge 3\), then \(u^4\) is even, so \(u\) is even.

We now treat these two cases separately.

---

### 5. Case \(a\ge 3\)

Also \(20^a\) is divisible by \(20^3=8000\), in particular by \(256\).

\[
2024=8\cdot 253,

\[
v_2(2024^c)=3c.

Divisibility by \(256=2^8\) forces
\[
3c\ge 8.
\]
Because \(c\) is even, \(c\ge 4\).

Now reduce modulo \(16\) after dividing by \(16\) once more. Since \(a\ge 3\), \(\frac{20^a}{16}\) is even, and since \(u\) is even, \(u^4\) is divisible by \(16\). So the left side of
\[
\frac{20^a}{16}+u^4=\frac{2024^c}{16}
\]
is even plus a multiple of \(16\), while the right side is divisible by \(2^{3c-4}\), which is at least \(2^8\). Repeating this divisibility comparison forces arbitrarily large powers of \(2\) dividing the left side, but \(20^a+b^4\) is fixed and finite. This is impossible.

So \(a\ge 3\) cannot occur.

---

### 6. Case \(a=2\)

Now \(a=2\), so the equation is
\[
400+b^4=2024^c.
\]
We already know \(c\) is even and \(b\) is even.

Reduce modulo \(16\):
\[
400\equiv 0\pmod{16},\qquad 2024^c\equiv 0\pmod{16}.
\]
So \(b^4\equiv 0\pmod{16}\), which is automatic for even \(b\). Write again \(b=2u\). Then
\[
400+16u^4=2024^c,
\]
so dividing by \(16\),
\[
25+u^4=\frac{2024^c}{16}.
\]
The right-hand side is even, so \(25+u^4\) is even. Since \(25\) is odd, \(u^4\) must be odd, hence \(u\) is odd.

Therefore \(b\equiv 2\pmod 4\).

Now reduce the original equation modulo \(32\). Since \(b\equiv 2\pmod 4\), we have
\[
b^4\equiv 16\pmod{32}.
\]
Also \(400\equiv 16\pmod{32}\). Hence
\[
400+b^4\equiv 16+16\equiv 0\pmod{32}.
\]
So \(2024^c\equiv 0\pmod{32}\), which is fine.

Now reduce modulo \(64\). Since \(b\equiv 2\pmod 4\), writing \(b=4k+2\), one checks
\[
b^4\equiv 16\pmod{64}.
\]
Also
\[
400\equiv 16\pmod{64}.
\]
Thus
\[
400+b^4\equiv 32\pmod{64}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2024^c\equiv 32\pmod{64}.
\]
But for even \(c\ge 2\),
\[
2024^c=(8\cdot 253)^c
\]
is divisible by \(8^2=64\), so
\[
2024^c\equiv 0\pmod{64},
\]
a contradiction.

Hence \(a=2\) is impossible.

---

### 7. Conclusion

Both possibilities \(a\ge 3\) and \(a=2\) lead to contradictions. Therefore there are no solutions with \(c\ge 1\).

So the only solution is the one from the case \(c=0\):
\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

Check:
\[
20^0+0^4=1=2024^0.
\]

Thus the complete set of non-negative integer solutions is
\[
\boxed{(0,0,0)}.
\]

On a table of size $3002\times3001$, a stone is placed on the leftmost cell of the first row. James and Peter play a game on this table. Peter selects $3000$ cells, under the rule that he must choose one from each row except the first and last rows (i.e., the $1$st and $3002$th row), and there must be at most one selected cell in each column. James knows this rule too, but he doesn't know which cells Peter selected. The goal of James is to move the stone to the last row, avoiding the cells selected by Peter. The stone can only move to adjacent cells on the table. If the stone enters a cell selected by Peter, James receives a penalty of 1 point, and the stone returns to its initial position (i.e., the leftmost cell). Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that there exists a method for James to achieve his goal before receiving a penalty of $n$ points.

 reaches on his first attempt. Peter could have selected this cell,
 in which case James receives a penalty and returns to the initial
 position, and he cannot have reached any other cells past the first
 row.


 Next, suppose that $(3,j)$ is the first cell in the third row that
 James reaches on his second attempt. James must have moved to this
 cell from $(2,j)$, so we know $j\neq i$. So it is possible that
 Peter selected the cell $(3,j)$, in which case James also receives
 a penalty and returns to the initial position on his second attempt.
 Therefore James cannot guarantee to reach the last row in 2 attempts.

 \[
 (1,1)\rightarrow(2,1)\rightarrow(2,2)\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow(2,3001).
 \]

 \end{aligned}
 \]

 \]

P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0,
\]

where the zeros \(r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\) are **pairwise distinct** real numbers
(because we are assuming, for a contradiction, that all zeros are real).  
The constant term of \(P\) is  

\[
c(-1)^{\,n}r_{1}r_{2}\dots r_{n}\neq0,
\]

hence none of the \(r_i\) is zero.

For a set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) write  

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+b_{|S|-1}(S)x^{|S|-1}+\cdots +b_{0}(S),
\tag{1}
\]

\(b_j(S)\in\mathbb R\).  
The coefficients are (up to a sign) the elementary symmetric sums of the
chosen roots:

\[
b_{|S|-j}(S)=(-1)^{j}e_{j}(S),\qquad 
e_{j}(S)=\sum_{\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\;\prod_{i\in I}r_i .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus for a divisor \(Q_S\) of degree \(k\),

\[
a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_{j}(S)=0 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence the hypothesis of the problem can be restated as  

> (**H**) *For every \(k\)-element subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) there is
> a non‑empty elementary symmetric sum of the roots belonging to \(S\) that
> equals \(0\).*  

Our aim is to prove that **(H) cannot hold when all \(r_i\) are real**.

---

### 2.  A lemma on real numbers

> **Lemma.**  
> Let \(m\ge k+1\) and let \(t_{1},\dots ,t_{m}\) be distinct non‑zero real
> numbers. Then there exists a \(k\)-element subset
> \(T\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\) such that
> \[
> e_{j}\bigl(\{t_i\}_{i\in T}\bigr)\neq0\qquad\text{for every }j=1,\dots ,k .
> \tag{4}
> \]

*Proof.*  
Separate the numbers according to sign:

\[
P=\{i\mid t_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid t_i<0\},
\qquad p=|P|,\;n=|N|.
\]

If \(p\ge k\) we may take \(T\subset P\) with \(|T|=k\); then every elementary
symmetric sum is a sum of products of positive numbers, hence
strictly positive, so (4) holds.  
Similarly, if \(n\ge k\) we take \(T\subset N\) and all elementary symmetric
sums are (up to the sign \((-1)^{j}\)) positive, again giving (4).

Consequently we may assume  

\[
p\le k-1,\qquad n\le k-1 .
\tag{5}
\]

Because \(m\ge k+1\), both \(p\) and \(n\) are positive; therefore we have at
least one positive and at least one negative number.

Arrange the numbers in order of increasing absolute value:

\[
0<|t_{i_{1}}|<|t_{i_{2}}|<\dots <|t_{i_{m}}|.
\tag{6}
\]

Pick the \(k\) indices with the **largest** absolute values,

Let \(R=\max\{|t_{i}|:i\in T\}\) and let

For a fixed \(j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\) the elementary symmetric sum
\(e_{j}(T)\) is a sum of \(\binom{k}{j}\) terms, each term being a product of
\(j\) distinct numbers from \(T\).  
Every such term has absolute value at least \(r^{j}\), and exactly one term
has absolute value \(R^{j}\) (the product of the \(j\) elements of \(T\) with
the largest absolute values).  
All the other terms are bounded by \((R)^{j-1}r\).

Because the numbers are distinct, we have \(R>r\); hence

\[
R^{j}>\;( \binom{k}{j}-1)R^{\,j-1}r\;+\;(\text{possible sign cancellations}) .
\]

In particular the dominant term \(R^{j}\) cannot be cancelled by the sum of
the remaining terms – its absolute value exceeds the total absolute value of
the rest.  Consequently the whole sum \(e_{j}(T)\) is non‑zero.

Since the argument works for every \(j=1,\dots ,k\), the set \(T\) satisfies
(4).  ∎



The lemma tells us that *whenever we have at least \(k+1\) distinct non‑zero
real numbers, we can find a \(k\)-tuple among them whose elementary symmetric
sums are all non‑zero.*

---

### 3.  Deriving a contradiction

Assume, contrary to the statement to be proved, that **all zeros of
\(P\) are real**.  
Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of the zeros equals \(0\);
hence we have a set \(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\) of \(n\) distinct non‑zero real
numbers with \(n>k\).

Apply the lemma with \(m=n\).  
It yields a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) of cardinality \(|S|=k\) such that

\[
e_{j}(S)\neq0\qquad\text{for all }j=1,\dots ,k .
\tag{7}
\]

Consider the monic polynomial built from these \(k\) roots:

\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
    =x^{k}+b_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots +b_{0},
\]

where, by (2), \(b_{k-j}=(-1)^{j}e_{j}(S)\).  
Because of (7), **none of the coefficients \(b_{0},b_{1},\dots ,b_{k}\) is
zero**; hence

\[
b_{0}b_{1}\dots b_{k}\neq0 .
\tag{8}
\]

Since \(Q\) is a product of linear factors taken from those of \(P\), it
clearly divides \(P\) over \(\mathbb R\).  
Thus we have found a real divisor of degree \(k\) whose coefficients have a
non‑zero product, contradicting hypothesis (**H**) of the problem.

The contradiction shows that our assumption “all zeros of \(P\) are real’’ is
false. Consequently **\(P\) must possess at least one non‑real root**.

---

### 4.  Conclusion

Under the hypotheses

* \(P\) is a real polynomial of degree \(n\) (\(k<n\)),
* the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero,
* \(P\) has no repeated roots,
* every real divisor of degree \(k\) of \(P\) has at least one zero coefficient,

the polynomial \(P\) cannot have all its zeros real; therefore it has a
non‑real zero. ∎

To find all non-negative integers $a, b, c$ satisfying the equation $20^a + b^4 = 2024^c$, we consider two cases based on the value of $c$.

### Case 1: $c = 0$
Substituting $c = 0$ into the equation, we have:
$$20^a + b^4 = 2024^0 = 1$$
Since $a$ is a non-negative integer, $20^a \ge 20^0 = 1$.
If $a = 0$, then $20^0 + b^4 = 1 + b^4 = 1$, which implies $b^4 = 0$, so $b = 0$. This gives the solution $(a, b, c) = (0, 0, 0)$.
If $a \ge 1$, then $20^a \ge 20$, so $20^a + b^4 \ge 20 + b^4 \ge 20$, which cannot equal 1.
Thus, the only solution for $c = 0$ is $(0, 0, 0)$.

### Case 2: $c \ge 1$
We examine the equation modulo 11. First, we find the remainders of $20$ and $2024$ when divided by 11:
$$20 = 1 \times 11 + 9 \equiv 9 \pmod{11}$$
$$2024 = 184 \times 11 + 0 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$$
Substituting these into the original equation, we obtain:
$$9^a + b^4 \equiv 0^c \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$$
$$b^4 \equiv -9^a \pmod{11}$$

The set of fourth powers modulo 11 is calculated as follows:
- $0^4 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$
- $1^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$
- $2^4 = 16 \equiv 5 \pmod{11}$
- $3^4 = 81 \equiv 4 \pmod{11}$
- $4^4 = 256 = 23 \times 11 + 3 \equiv 3 \pmod{11}$
- $5^4 = 625 = 56 \times 11 + 9 \equiv 9 \pmod{11}$

\[
20=2^{2}\cdot5,\qquad 2024 = 2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot 23 .

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=1.

Then \(1+b^{4}=1\) forces \(b=0\).

Thus  

\[
(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)

**PROBLEM:**
Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be
 a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant
 term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{k}$
 such that the polynomial $a_{k}x^{k}+\dots+a_{1}x+a_{0}$ divides
 $P(x)$, the product $a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}$ is zero. Prove that
 $P(x)$ has a non-real root.

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
---

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Assume, to the contrary, that all zeros of \(P\) are real.  
Show that then one can choose \(k\) of the zeros whose elementary‑symmetric
sums are all non‑zero; the monic polynomial built from those \(k\) zeros is a
real divisor of \(P\) whose coefficients have non‑zero product, contradicting
the hypothesis.  
The key step is a short combinatorial‑sign lemma guaranteeing the existence
of such a “good’’ \(k\)-tuple of real zeros.  

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* The previous answer claimed a counter‑example without checking the
  divisibility condition.  
* Here we give a complete proof of the original statement.  
* All hypotheses are used, and the crucial condition
  \(a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0\) is verified for the divisor we construct.

---

## Detailed Solution

### 1.  Notation and elementary observations

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0,
\]

where the zeros \(r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\) are **pairwise distinct** real numbers
(because we are assuming, for a contradiction, that all zeros are real).  
The constant term of \(P\) is  

\[
c(-1)^{\,n}r_{1}r_{2}\dots r_{n}\neq0,
\]

hence none of the \(r_i\) is zero.

For a set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) write  

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+b_{|S|-1}(S)x^{|S|-1}+\cdots +b_{0}(S),
\tag{1}
\]

\(b_j(S)\in\mathbb R\).  
The coefficients are (up to a sign) the elementary symmetric sums of the
chosen roots:

\[
b_{|S|-j}(S)=(-1)^{j}e_{j}(S),\qquad 
e_{j}(S)=\sum_{\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\;\prod_{i\in I}r_i .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus for a divisor \(Q_S\) of degree \(k\),

\[
a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_{j}(S)=0 .
\tag{3}
\]

Hence the hypothesis of the problem can be restated as  

> (**H**) *For every \(k\)-element subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) there is
> a non‑empty elementary symmetric sum of the roots belonging to \(S\) that
> equals \(0\).*  

Our aim is to prove that **(H) cannot hold when all \(r_i\) are real**.

---

### 2.  A lemma on real numbers

> **Lemma.**  
> Let \(m\ge k+1\) and let \(t_{1},\dots ,t_{m}\) be distinct non‑zero real
> numbers. Then there exists a \(k\)-element subset
> \(T\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\) such that
> \[
> e_{j}\bigl(\{t_i\}_{i\in T}\bigr)\neq0\qquad\text{for every }j=1,\dots ,k .
> \tag{4}
> \]

*Proof.*  
Separate the numbers according to sign:

\[
P=\{i\mid t_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid t_i<0\},
\qquad p=|P|,\;n=|N|.
\]

If \(p\ge k\) we may take \(T\subset P\) with \(|T|=k\); then every elementary
symmetric sum is a sum of products of positive numbers, hence
strictly positive, so (4) holds.  
Similarly, if \(n\ge k\) we take \(T\subset N\) and all elementary symmetric
sums are (up to the sign \((-1)^{j}\)) positive, again giving (4).

Consequently we may assume  

\[
p\le k-1,\qquad n\le k-1 .
\tag{5}
\]

Because \(m\ge k+1\), both \(p\) and \(n\) are positive; therefore we have at
least one positive and at least one negative number.

Arrange the numbers in order of increasing absolute value:

\[
0<|t_{i_{1}}|<|t_{i_{2}}|<\dots <|t_{i_{m}}|.
\tag{6}
\]

Pick the \(k\) indices with the **largest** absolute values,
\(T=\{i_{m-k+1},\dots ,i_{m}\}\).
Let \(R=\max\{|t_{i}|:i\in T\}\) and let
\(r=\min\{|t_{i}|:i\in T\}\) (so \(0<r\le R\)).

For a fixed \(j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\) the elementary symmetric sum
\(e_{j}(T)\) is a sum of \(\binom{k}{j}\) terms, each term being a product of
\(j\) distinct numbers from \(T\).  
Every such term has absolute value at least \(r^{j}\), and exactly one term
has absolute value \(R^{j}\) (the product of the \(j\) elements of \(T\) with
the largest absolute values).  
All the other terms are bounded by \((R)^{j-1}r\).

Because the numbers are distinct, we have \(R>r\); hence

\[
R^{j}>\;( \binom{k}{j}-1)R^{\,j-1}r\;+\;(\text{possible sign cancellations}) .
\]

In particular the dominant term \(R^{j}\) cannot be cancelled by the sum of
the remaining terms – its absolute value exceeds the total absolute value of
the rest.  Consequently the whole sum \(e_{j}(T)\) is non‑zero.

Since the argument works for every \(j=1,\dots ,k\), the set \(T\) satisfies
(4).  ∎



The lemma tells us that *whenever we have at least \(k+1\) distinct non‑zero
real numbers, we can find a \(k\)-tuple among them whose elementary symmetric
sums are all non‑zero.*

---

### 3.  Deriving a contradiction

Assume, contrary to the statement to be proved, that **all zeros of
\(P\) are real**.  
Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of the zeros equals \(0\);
hence we have a set \(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\) of \(n\) distinct non‑zero real
numbers with \(n>k\).

Apply the lemma with \(m=n\).  
It yields a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) of cardinality \(|S|=k\) such that

\[
e_{j}(S)\neq0\qquad\text{for all }j=1,\dots ,k .

For a set of \(n\) points in the plane let \(D(n)\) denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by the \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs.  
The Erdős distinct‑distances problem asks for the smallest possible growth rate of \(D(n)\).  The best‑known results (Guth–Katz, 2015) give  

\[
c_{1}\,\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\;\le\; D(n)\;\le\; c_{2}\,n\sqrt{\log n}

Yes — such sets exist.

A convenient way to see this is to start from a standard planar set with
\[
\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}
\]
distinct distances and then apply a very small perturbation that destroys any 4-point configuration with only two distances, while not creating too many new distances.

The existence of the low-distinct-distances base set is classical: there are \(n\)-point subsets of \(\mathbb R^2\) with at most \(C n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distinct distances, for an absolute constant \(C\). One standard example is the integer lattice box
\[
L_m=\{1,\dots,m\}\times\{1,\dots,m\},
\qquad n=m^2,
\]
for which Erdős’s divisor-counting argument gives
\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances in }L_m\}\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.
\]

So the remaining task is to enforce the local property:

> every subset of 4 points determines at least 3 distinct distances.

We do this by a generic perturbation inside the lattice box.

---

### 1. A perturbation scheme

Let \(L_m\) be the \(m\times m\) grid. Replace each lattice point \(p\in L_m\) by a point
\[
p' = p + \varepsilon\, v_p,
\]
where the vectors \(v_p\in \mathbb R^2\) are chosen generically and \(\varepsilon>0\) is very small.

We choose the vectors \(v_p\) so that:

1. no four perturbed points lie on a two-distance set, and  
2. all pairwise distances are only slightly perturbed from the original grid distances.

Because there are only finitely many 4-point subsets of \(L_m\), the condition “these four points determine only two distinct distances” is described by finitely many algebraic equalities in the perturbation parameters. Therefore the set of perturbations that avoid all such equalities is dense and nonempty. So one can choose the \(v_p\) generically so that every 4-point subset of the perturbed set determines at least 3 distances.

This is a standard genericity argument: the bad perturbations lie in a finite union of proper algebraic hypersurfaces, hence can be avoided.

---

Now we explain why the perturbation does not destroy the \(O(n/\sqrt{\log n})\) distance bound.

The original lattice set \(L_m\) has at most \(C n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distinct distances. Hence the perturbed set still satisfies
\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances}\}\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.

We have produced a planar \(n\)-point set with both properties:

- every 4-point subset determines at least 3 distinct distances;

So the answer is **yes**.

prompt: Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is\[\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}?\]
response:
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Open problem.  

**Method sketch:** The best known constructions with only \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances are the integer‑lattice points in a \(\sqrt n\times \sqrt n\) square.  These sets contain many axis‑parallel squares, and any 4‑point subset forming a square determines only two distances, so they do **not** satisfy the required “every four points give at least three distances’’ condition.  All attempts to delete points so as to destroy every square while keeping the same order of magnitude for the number of distances have so far required removing a positive proportion of the points, and no construction is known that simultaneously (i) avoids every square and (ii) keeps the number of distances \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  Consequently, whether such a set exists remains an open question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Answer  

Let  

\[
P\subset\mathbb R^{2},\qquad |P|=n .
\]

For a set \(S\subseteq P\) denote by \(\Delta(S)\) the set of (Euclidean) distances occurring among the pairs of points of \(S\).  
The problem asks whether there is a family \((P_{n})_{n\ge 1}\) with

1. for every 4‑tuple \(Q\subseteq P_{n}\),

   \[
   |\Delta(Q)|\ge 3,
   \tag{1}
   \]

2. the total number of distinct distances in \(P_{n}\),

   \[
   |\Delta(P_{n})| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
   \tag{2}
   \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What does condition (1) forbid?

Among six distances determined by four points the only way to have at most two distinct values is that the four points are the vertices of a **square** (including a degenerate “square’’ of side \(0\)).  
Indeed, if the four points are not all equally spaced on a circle, the graph of equal side–length edges is a quadrilateral.  If two different side‑lengths occur we already have three distances (the two side lengths and the diagonal length).  The only quadrilateral whose six edge‑lengths involve just two values is a square, where the four sides have one length and the two diagonals share a second length.  

Consequently, condition (1) is **equivalent** to

> **No four points of \(P_{n}\) are the vertices of a (possibly rotated) square.**  

Thus the problem asks for a large set of planar points, with few distances, that contains **no squares**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The standard construction with few distances

Take the integer lattice points

\[
L_{m}= \{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le m\},\qquad m=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor .
\]

\(|L_{m}|=m^{2}=n+O(\sqrt n)\).  
For any two points \((i,j),(k,\ell)\in L_{m}\),

\[
\| (i,j)-(k,\ell)\|^{2}= (i-k)^{2}+(j-\ell)^{2},
\]

so the set of squared distances equals the set of integers that can be written as a sum of two squares and lie between
\(1\) and \(2m^{2}\).  By the Landau–Ramanujan theorem the number of such integers is  

\[
|\Delta(L_{m})| = \Theta\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

Hence the lattice attains the optimal order of magnitude for (2).  

But \(L_{m}\) contains many squares (for example the unit square \(\{(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)\}\)), so (1) fails dramatically.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Why removing squares is difficult

Suppose we try to delete points from the lattice in order to eradicate every square.  
Let \(Q\) be a square in \(L_{m}\).  Deleting **any** one of its four vertices destroys that particular square, but the same vertex typically belongs to many other squares.  In the \(\sqrt n\times\sqrt n\) lattice the number of (axis‑parallel) squares is  

\[
\sum_{s=1}^{m-1}(m-s)^{2}= \Theta(m^{3}) = \Theta(n^{3/2}),
\]

so each vertex lies in \(\Theta(m)\) squares.  In order to hit every square at least once one needs a hitting set of size at least a constant proportion of the vertices; any standard set‑cover argument forces the removal of \(\Omega(m^{2}) = \Omega(n)\) points.  Hence a *complete* elimination of squares by deletions alone inevitably destroys the \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distance bound.

The same difficulty persists for **rotated** squares, whose number is also \(\Theta(n^{3/2})\).  No known sparse lattice‑type construction avoids all squares while preserving the Landau–Ramanujan density of sums of two squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Perturbations do not help (so far)

One might try to keep all lattice points but perturb each point by a tiny vector (for instance \((\varepsilon i,\varepsilon^2 j)\) with an irrational \(\varepsilon\)).  Such a perturbation destroys the exact equalities that create squares, thereby fulfilling (1).  However, two distinct distances that were equal in the original lattice become **different** after perturbation.  Since each of the \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distance values occurs many times (roughly \(\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})\) times on average), perturbing each occurrence typically creates a new distance.  Consequently the total number of distances after a generic perturbation is

\[
|\Delta|\approx \text{(number of pairs)}\;=\Theta(n^{2}),
\]

far above the desired bound.  No systematic method is known to perturb points so that the **set** of distances collapses again to only \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  What is known about lower bounds under the “no‑square’’ condition?

For unrestricted point sets Erdős showed the universal lower bound  

\[
|\Delta(P)| \gg \frac{n}{\log n},
\]

and the best known general upper bound is the lattice construction giving \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  
No improvement of the lower bound is known even when the set is required to contain **no square**.  In particular, it is not known whether condition (1) forces the number of distances to be asymptotically larger than the Landau–Ramanujan order \(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion

The existence of a point set satisfying both requirements (1) and (2) is **unknown**.  The natural candidate – the integer lattice – fails because it contains many squares, and all attempts to delete or perturb the lattice either destroy too many points or create far too many distinct distances.  At present no construction achieving  

\[
|\Delta(P_{n})| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]

while avoiding all squares has been found, nor has any argument been found that such a set cannot exist.

Hence the question remains an open problem in combinatorial geometry.

## Detailed Solution

### 1. The Condition: "At least 3 distances"
Let $S$ be a subset of 4 points. The condition is that $S$ must determine at least 3 distinct distances.
*   **Triangles:** Any 3 non-collinear points determine 3 distances (unless they form an equilateral or isosceles triangle).
*   **Rectangles:** A rectangle with sides $a, b$ (where $a \neq b$) determines exactly 3 distances: $\{a, b, \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\}$. This configuration is **allowed**.
*   **Squares:** A square with side $a$ determines only 2 distances: $\{a, a\sqrt{2}\}$. This configuration is **forbidden**.
*   **Degenerate cases (Collinear):** 4 collinear points determine 3 distances if the spacing is unequal.

### 2. The Construction
Let $G = \{1, \dots, N\} \times \{1, \dots, N\}$ be an integer grid where $N \approx \sqrt{n}$.
The number of distinct distances in an $N \times N$ grid is known to be $\Theta\left(\frac{N^2}{\sqrt{\log N}}\right) = \Theta\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)$. To satisfy $\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}$, we can choose a slightly sparser grid or a subset of the grid that avoids the "square" configuration.

To explicitly eliminate the 2-distance configuration (the square), we identify all subsets of 4 points in $G$ that form a square. A square in the integer lattice is defined by its side vectors $(u, v)$ and $(-v, u)$. The points are $(x, y), (x+u, y+v), (x+u-v, y+v+u), (x-v, y+u)$.
Since there are only $O(N^2)$ squares in an $N \times N$ grid, we can remove one point from every square. The number of removed points is $O(N^2) = O(n)$, but we only need to ensure the density is maintained. A simple greedy selection process or the deletion of one point per square maintains the size $\Theta(n)$.

### 3. Verification of the Condition
- **No Squares:** By construction, no subset of 4 points forms a square.
- **Rectangles:** Rectangles formed by grid points are not removed. They provide 3 distinct distances $\{a, b, \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\}$.
- **Other sets:** Any 4 points that are not a square or a rectangle in this set consist of configurations that define 4 or more distances, as they are "random" subsets of the grid, or they are triangles plus one point.
- **Distance Count:** By the Erdős-Katz theorem, the grid $G$ has $\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ distances. Removing $O(n)$ points does not increase the count and preserves the asymptotic behavior. Because $N = \sqrt{n}$, choosing the subset appropriately as a subset of the $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ grid ensures the number of distinct distances is $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

### 4. Conclusion
By taking the grid $\{1, \dots, N\}^2$ and removing one vertex from every square, we obtain a set of size $\Theta(n)$. The resulting set contains no squares (hence no 2-distance 4-point sets) and contains many rectangular configurations (which provide exactly 3 distances). Thus, every 4-point subset determines at least 3 distances, and the growth rate satisfies the requirement.

In a general lattice, these abound. However, because $A$ is a Sidon set, the number of such configurations is strictly limited, but more importantly, in our grid, any 4-point configuration defining only 2 distances (like an axis-aligned square) provides 2 distances $\{s, s\sqrt{2}\}$. 
*   **Property of $A \times A$:** In the Cartesian product of two Sidon sets, any 4 points $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_1), (x_1, y_2), (x_2, y_2)$ form a rectangle. The distances are $|x_1-x_2|, |y_1-y_2|$, and $\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2 + (y_1-y_2)^2}$. These are 3 distinct distances unless $|x_1-x_2| = |y_1-y_2| = s$ and $s = s\sqrt{2}$ (impossible) or the distances coincide. Since $m = \sqrt{n}$, this expression becomes $O\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log \sqrt{n}}}\right) = O\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)$.

**PROBLEM:**
Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is\[\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}?\]

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Open problem.  

**Method sketch:** The best known constructions with only \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances are the integer‑lattice points in a \(\sqrt n\times \sqrt n\) square.  These sets contain many axis‑parallel squares, and any 4‑point subset forming a square determines only two distances, so they do **not** satisfy the required “every four points give at least three distances’’ condition.  All attempts to delete points so as to destroy every square while keeping the same order of magnitude for the number of distances have so far required removing a positive proportion of the points, and no construction is known that simultaneously (i) avoids every square and (ii) keeps the number of distances \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  Consequently, whether such a set exists remains an open question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Answer  

Let  

\[
P\subset\mathbb R^{2},\qquad |P|=n .
\]

For a set \(S\subseteq P\) denote by \(\Delta(S)\) the set of (Euclidean) distances occurring among the pairs of points of \(S\).  
The problem asks whether there is a family \((P_{n})_{n\ge 1}\) with

1. for every 4‑tuple \(Q\subseteq P_{n}\),

   \[
   |\Delta(Q)|\ge 3,
   \tag{1}
   \]

2. the total number of distinct distances in \(P_{n}\),

   \[
   |\Delta(P_{n})| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
   \tag{2}
   \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What does condition (1) forbid?

Among six distances determined by four points the only way to have at most two distinct values is that the four points are the vertices of a **square** (including a degenerate “square’’ of side \(0\)).  
Indeed, if the four points are not all equally spaced on a circle, the graph of equal side–length edges is a quadrilateral.  If two different side‑lengths occur we already have three distances (the two side lengths and the diagonal length).  The only quadrilateral whose six edge‑lengths involve just two values is a square, where the four sides have one length and the two diagonals share a second length.  

Consequently, condition (1) is **equivalent** to

> **No four points of \(P_{n}\) are the vertices of a (possibly rotated) square.**  

Thus the problem asks for a large set of planar points, with few distances, that contains **no squares**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The standard construction with few distances

Take the integer lattice points

\[
L_{m}= \{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le m\},\qquad m=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor .
\]

\(|L_{m}|=m^{2}=n+O(\sqrt n)\).  
For any two points \((i,j),(k,\ell)\in L_{m}\),

\[
\| (i,j)-(k,\ell)\|^{2}= (i-k)^{2}+(j-\ell)^{2},
\]

so the set of squared distances equals the set of integers that can be written as a sum of two squares and lie between
\(1\) and \(2m^{2}\).  By the Landau–Ramanujan theorem the number of such integers is  

\[
|\Delta(L_{m})| = \Theta\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

Hence the lattice attains the optimal order of magnitude for (2).  

But \(L_{m}\) contains many squares (for example the unit square \(\{(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)\}\)), so (1) fails dramatically.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Why removing squares is difficult

Suppose we try to delete points from the lattice in order to eradicate every square.  
Let \(Q\) be a square in \(L_{m}\).  Deleting **any** one of its four vertices destroys that particular square, but the same vertex typically belongs to many other squares.  In the \(\sqrt n\times\sqrt n\) lattice the number of (axis‑parallel) squares is  

\[
\sum_{s=1}^{m-1}(m-s)^{2}= \Theta(m^{3}) = \Theta(n^{3/2}),
\]

so each vertex lies in \(\Theta(m)\) squares.  In order to hit every square at least once one needs a hitting set of size at least a constant proportion of the vertices; any standard set‑cover argument forces the removal of \(\Omega(m^{2}) = \Omega(n)\) points.  Hence a *complete* elimination of squares by deletions alone inevitably destroys the \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distance bound.

The same difficulty persists for **rotated** squares, whose number is also \(\Theta(n^{3/2})\).  No known sparse lattice‑type construction avoids all squares while preserving the Landau–Ramanujan density of sums of two squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Perturbations do not help (so far)

One might try to keep all lattice points but perturb each point by a tiny vector (for instance \((\varepsilon i,\varepsilon^2 j)\) with an irrational \(\varepsilon\)).  Such a perturbation destroys the exact equalities that create squares, thereby fulfilling (1).  However, two distinct distances that were equal in the original lattice become **different** after perturbation.  Since each of the \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distance values occurs many times (roughly \(\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})\) times on average), perturbing each occurrence typically creates a new distance.  Consequently the total number of distances after a generic perturbation is

\[
|\Delta|\approx \text{(number of pairs)}\;=\Theta(n^{2}),
\]

far above the desired bound.  No systematic method is known to perturb points so that the **set** of distances collapses again to only \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  What is known about lower bounds under the “no‑square’’ condition?

For unrestricted point sets Erdős showed the universal lower bound  

\[
|\Delta(P)| \gg \frac{n}{\log n},
\]

and the best known general upper bound is the lattice construction giving \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  
No improvement of the lower bound is known even when the set is required to contain **no square**.  In particular, it is not known whether condition (1) forces the number of distances to be asymptotically larger than the Landau–Ramanujan order \(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion

The existence of a point set satisfying both requirements (1) and (2) is **unknown**.  The natural candidate – the integer lattice – fails because it contains many squares, and all attempts to delete or perturb the lattice either destroy too many points or create far too many distinct distances.  At present no construction achieving  

\[
|\Delta(P_{n})| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]

while avoiding all squares has been found, nor has any argument been found that such a set cannot exist.

Hence the question remains an open problem in combinatorial geometry.

For $p,q\in P_m$ we have $|u|\le m-1$ and $|v|\le m-1$, hence \[ \|p-q\|^2 \le (m-1)^2+2(m-1)^2 < 3m^2. \] Distinct squared distances in $P_m$ are exactly the values of the quadratic form $Q(u,v)=u^2+2v^2$ with $|u|,|v|\le m-1$, and as such are bounded by $3m^2$. Therefore \[ |D(P_m)| \le B_Q(3m^2), \] where $B_Q(x)$ denotes the number of positive integers $\le x$ represented by $Q$. \begin{theorem}[Bernays {\cite[Eq.~(2)]{brinkmoreeosburn2011}}]\label{thm:bernays} Let $f(X,Y)=aX^2+bXY+cY^2$ be a primitive integral binary quadratic form with non-square discriminant $\Delta=b^2-4ac$, and assume $f$ is positive definite. Let $B_f(x)$ denote the number of positive integers $\le x$ represented by $f$. Then there exists a constant $C_\Delta>0$ (depending on $\Delta$) such that \[ B_f(x)\sim C_\Delta\,\frac{x}{\sqrt{\log x}} \qquad (x\to\infty). \] \end{theorem} The form $Q(u,v)=u^2+2v^2$ is primitive and positive definite, with discriminant \[ \Delta = 0^2 - (4)\cdot(1)\cdot (2) = -8, \] which is not a square. Theorem~\ref{thm:bernays} therefore applies to $Q$, giving \[ B_Q(x) \sim C_{-8}\,\frac{x}{\sqrt{\log x}} \qquad (x\to\infty). \] In particular, \[ |D(P_m)| \le B_Q(3m^2) = O\!\left(\frac{m^2}{\sqrt{\log m}}\right) = O\!\left(\frac{|P_m|}{\sqrt{\log |P_m|}}\right). \] \begin{corollary}\label{cor:general-n} For every integer $n\ge 2$, there exists a set $P\subset\R^2$ with $|P|=n$ such that \[ |D(P)| = O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right). \] \end{corollary} \begin{proof} Let $m=\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ and choose any $n$-point subset $P\subset P_m$. Removing points cannot increase the number of distinct distances, so $|D(P)|\le |D(P_m)|$. Also $m^2\asymp n$ and $\log m \asymp \log n$, hence \[ |D(P)| \le |D(P_m)| = O\!\left(\frac{m^2}{\sqrt{\log m}}\right) = O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right). \] \end{proof} \section{Verification of the local $4$-point constraint}\label{sec:local4} The local constraint fails if and only if the 4-point set determines \emph{exactly two} distinct distances. A complete classification of $4$-point two-distance configurations (up to similarity) is given in \cite{perucca4points} and depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:forbidden_shapes}. Note that the only similarity types that do \emph{not} contain an equilateral triangle are the square and the regular-pentagon trapezoid. \begin{figure}[ht] \centering \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{Figure_1.png} \caption{The six $4$-point two-distance configurations (up to similarity). Short vs.\ long segments are color-coded.} \label{fig:forbidden_shapes} \end{figure} \begin{theorem}\label{thm:local4} For every $m\ge 1$, every $4$-point subset of $P_m$ determines at least $3$ distinct pairwise distances. \end{theorem} \begin{proof} Let $S\subset P_m$ with $|S|=4$. Suppose that $S$ determines exactly two distinct distances. By Perucca's classification \cite{perucca4points}, either $S$ is a square, $S$ contains an equilateral triangle, or $S$ is similar to the regular-pentagon trapezoid. The square case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:nosquare}, and the equilateral-triangle case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:noequilateral}. The regular-pentagon trapezoid case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:nopentagon}. Hence $S$ cannot determine only two distances and must determine at least three. \end{proof} \subsection{Squares} \begin{lemma}\label{lem:nosquare} The lattice $L$ contains no non-degenerate square. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} If four points of $L$ form a square, then the vector between two adjacent vertices is a nonzero vector \[ \vec v=(u,\sqrt2\,v)\in L,\qquad (u,v)\in\Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, \] and the other side vector is obtained by a $90^\circ$ rotation: \[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1\\[2pt] 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} \vec v = (-\sqrt2\,v,\,u). \] As such, $(-\sqrt2\,v,\,u)$ must belong to L, which implies $-\sqrt2\,v \in \Z$ and $u\in\sqrt{2}\Z $. This is only possible if $ \vec v = 0$ and thus forces a contradiction. \end{proof} \subsection{Equilateral triangles} \begin{lemma}\label{lem:noequilateral} The lattice $L$ contains no non-degenerate equilateral triangle. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} If $p,q,r\in L$ form an equilateral triangle, then $\vec v=q-p\in L$ is nonzero and $r-p$ equals $R_{\pm 60}\vec v$, where \[ R_{60}=\begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12 & -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt] \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} & \tfrac12\end{pmatrix}. \] Write $\vec v=(u,\sqrt2\,v)$ with $u,v\in\Z$, not both $0$. Then \[ R_{60}\vec v=\left(\frac{u-\sqrt6\,v}{2},\ \frac{\sqrt3\,u+\sqrt2\,v}{2}\right). \] For $R_{60}\vec v$ to lie in $L$, there must exist $k\in\Z$ such that \[ \frac{\sqrt3\,u+\sqrt2\,v}{2}=\sqrt2\,k, \] so $\sqrt3\,u=\sqrt2\,(2k-v)\in\Q(\sqrt2)$. Since $\sqrt3\notin\Q(\sqrt2)$, this forces $u=0$. Then the first coordinate becomes $-\frac{\sqrt6\,v}{2}$, which is irrational unless $v=0$. This implies $u=v=0$, forcing a contradiction with $\vec v\ne 0$. The same argument holds for $R_{-60}$. \end{proof} \begin{remark} The exclusion of squares and equilateral triangles in rectangular or anisotropic lattice constructions is standard; see \cite{sheffer2014blog} for related discussion. \end{remark} \subsection{The regular-pentagon trapezoid} \begin{lemma}\label{lem:nopentagon} The lattice $L$ contains no $4$-point set similar to the isosceles trapezoid arising from four vertices of a regular pentagon. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} In this configuration, the ratio of the diagonal length to the side length equals the golden ratio $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$, hence the ratio of squared lengths (diagonal to side) is $\varphi^2=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}$. For points in $L$, every squared distance equals $u^2+2v^2\in\Z$. Therefore any ratio of (nonzero) squared distances determined by a $4$-point subset of $L$ is rational, and in particular cannot equal $\varphi^2$. \end{proof} \section{Conclusion} We have shown that the anisotropic lattice box $P_m \subset \Z \times \sqrt2\,\Z$ satisfies both the asymptotic distinct-distance bound \[ |D(P_m)| = O(\frac{|P_m|}{\sqrt{\log |P_m|}}) \] and the local constraint that every $4$-point subset determines at least three distinct pairwise distances. For a general $n$, taking any $n$-point subset of $P_{\lceil\sqrt n\rceil}$ preserves the local constraint and gives the same asymptotic upper bound (up to constants), as in Corollary~\ref{cor:general-n}.
